entry.title: Opinion: Cutting off the Lizard’s Tail: A Flawed Perspective

link.title: Opinion: Cutting off the Lizard’s Tail: A Flawed Perspective

entry.content:
I guess I should start by saying that I’m in a much better place now than I was two years ago. Even compared to a year ago, things have been changing and moving so fast that it all feels a little surreal. I’ve had more opportunities that I wouldn’t have believed possible not long ago and I find myself to be one of the only bottlenecks left to my own success. And that makes this perhaps a little strange to write, maybe even self-indulgent. But that’s also why I think it’s important for me to write this right now, while I still remember what it was like to struggle to even get a foot in the door, to not even know what I know or what I don’t know, and how it feels to have people actually give you a chance.

I’ve done academic research for less than two years at this point, and there’s obviously a lot I don’t understand, especially what happens in the room where it happens. I don’t claim to have some sort of magic bullet for the problems I talk about below, and maybe there isn’t even a solution that would satisfy everyone. And yet I write this in a moment of clarity in hopes that this will reach people much more capable and powerful than I am, so that it can add another perspective to the ensemble.

So take this as a terribly flawed perspective from someone who probably isn’t seeing the full picture. This is how I see it.

As an undergrad at UIUC, I wanted to do research. After all, my main motivation coming into a computer science and linguistics degree was to create something like Baymax, and I wasn’t going to get there by learning how to do LeetCode. But having just “entered the field”, by which I mean I’d just finished reading a couple papers from Percy Liang’s group about LLM agents going off and organizing a birthday party together (or at least that’s how I remember it), my interests were all over the place. I emailed practically every professor that seemed to be working on something even remotely related. At this point I had built personal projects, was the president of a decently sized coding student organization, competed in hackathons and datathons, and even presented smaller projects at student research symposiums. Unlike others around me, I didn’t have anyone to tell me what I had to do to get into research, and I didn’t even know about what I didn’t know, so I guess in my mind I was doing everything I could think of.

But even after all that, I still couldn’t find a way in. I would have been happy to shadow someone or help run experiments, whatever was needed of me. I wasn’t asking for a salary or a recommendation letter. I just wanted my foot in the door.

I say this, but I guess it’s not like those professors owed me anything. I understand this. I’m sure they had much more on their plate than I could imagine, writing grants and teaching and whatnot. I’m sure some of my cold emails could have been better, and I probably wasn’t as ready to contribute as I thought. But at the same time, if not at one of the top research institutes in the US, how was I supposed to get my start?

Eventually a professor gave me a chance around 3 years into my search (FOCAL Lab shoutout!), mostly because I happened to be close to one of his favorite students. I’m very grateful for that. I learned much from this experience that I carry with me today, and of course it changed my path a great deal. But it’s not like I suddenly became a better researcher because I knew the right person. I was still the same student who had been sending cold emails for years. And I wonder what would have happened if I hadn’t known that student, and how many people are in the same spot but never meet the right person.

UIUC is a well-regarded research university with a lot of resources. I think overall I had a good education and had people around me with similar interests, and I had room to learn on my own. And if despite all this, getting started was that hard for me, I can only imagine what it’s like for someone at a smaller university or without an academic network. The same goes for people trying to enter the world of research on their own.

It’s strange how early we expect people to have research experience nowadays. Competitive Master’s and PhD applications put a lot of weight on prior research experience, and prestigious undergraduate research positions often explicitly favor students who have already worked in a lab or published. I’ve even been rejected from a student organization because I didn’t have any publications. You end up needing research experience to get research experience.

I suppose things get better when people are able to get past that first barrier, as they then often get access to opportunities that make the next barriers easier to overcome. This is known as the Matthew effect: a 2018 study found that early-career researchers who won a grant went on to get more than twice the funding over the next eight years compared to those that didn’t, even when the two groups had almost identical review scores. Once you’ve had that first opportunity, people have something to go off of. You have people who can vouch for you and, more importantly, a better understanding of how things work. Before that, you’re kinda just asking someone to take a chance on you.

And when getting those initial opportunities becomes increasingly competitive, I think it’s almost inevitable that people start looking for other ways in.

As research experience and publications become increasingly important for getting into graduate school, I’ve also noticed that there’s basically an entire industry around charging high school students thousands of dollars for publications.

One such example is Algoverse, which apparently costs $4,325 to participate in. On one hand, I’m sure that running something like this costs a considerable amount of money, and I’m sure it’s not impossible for good work to come out of a program like this. After all, if someone is capable of making a meaningful scientific contribution at sixteen, more power to them. My concern is more with the idea itself: the incentive structure building up around research.

I may be jumping to conclusions, but considering that this is something that most Master’s students I’ve talked to struggle with, I wonder how many students are participating because they actually have a question they’re curious about, and how many are doing it because they think having a paper will help them get into a better university. And considering that this is happening because admissions committees reward research experience, and research experience is increasingly difficult to get without already having some, it’s not entirely right to blame the students for this either.

Needless to say, those who can afford to pay thousands of dollars for papers are probably not the people who would have struggled much to find opportunities to begin with. It’s another way that existing advantages widen the gap over time.

Let’s say someone finds a question they’re excited about. Arguably, this is already a pretty high bar when starting out. But on top of this, let’s say they have no official advisor, or their institution has little funding. In machine learning, the research itself can be quite expensive due to compute and potential API access to closed-source models. But I suppose at this stage, it is not impossible to get a small compute grant or something along those lines. But even if they somehow end up with something worth sharing despite these obstacles, they then run into a second set of costs. Conference registration regularly costs hundreds of dollars. Add flights, a hotel, food, and maybe even a visa, and a single international conference can easily rack up a huge bill. For independent researchers or people at underfunded institutions, especially in lower-income countries, the cost can make attendance effectively impossible.

It’s not like nothing is done about this; NeurIPS and ICML both run financial assistance programs, but the programs leave something to be desired. NeurIPS 2026 financial assistance can cover registration and hotel, but not travel, and ICML 2026 also offered help with registration and accommodation but not airfare. Even with an accepted paper and financial assistance, it’s quite realistic that you might not be able to afford the trip.

Much of a conference’s value in my opinion comes not from the event itself but from the conversations, where you can get feedback and meet possible collaborators. If you can go, your paper can lead to new opportunities. If you can’t, you get a line on your CV and end up back at square one. It’s not just missing a conference. It’s missing an opportunity to meet the people who might make the next opportunity possible.

Of course, I’m sure running a conference is expensive. There’s a lot of staff and logistics involved, often working full time to work out venue contracts and whatnot, and all of that costs money. And I’m sure this is what the registration fees go towards funding. At the same time, according to its public nonprofit tax filings, the NeurIPS Foundation had about $22.3 million in net assets at the end of its fiscal year in May 2025, after about $15.2 million in revenue and $10 million in expenses. That’s a lot of money to be sitting on when there are countless people at every conference who end up not being able to attend due to financial restrictions and there are talented individuals who have no way to break into the field. Since I haven’t come across anyone who knew about this while writing this post, maybe it’s at least worth discussing.

Academia is struggling, especially in machine learning, and from there especially in LLM/agent related fields. I think most people in the know would agree with that.

NeurIPS went from 9,467 submissions in 2020 to 21,575 in 2025, more than double in five years. The reviewer pool has grown somewhat too, thanks to reciprocal reviewing, but it seems almost inevitable that review quality slips.

Reviewers are usually overworked PhD students with a conflict of interest where the game-theoretic way to “play the game” seems to be to just reject your entire pile to marginally increase the chances that your own paper gets in. It’s like some nerdy version of the prisoner’s dilemma. There is a world where everyone reviews thoroughly for each other and contributes to progress and the accumulation of knowledge, but alas, it’s not the one we’re living in. Even if we don’t go that far, with LLMs making it easier than ever to produce something that is “paper-shaped”, it calls for changes to how we look at academia.

I guess for one, the goal of research shouldn’t be to get your paper accepted at a conference. Research should be done to find out something new, contributing to the pool of knowledge. Publications are just one way to share this. Many senior researchers have thus been calling for a shift away from conferences, towards things like blog posts and Twitter threads to be spread around the community so that we can avoid going through one overloaded submission cycle.

And I think this is all well and good; it would likely make things a lot easier to “filter out” “slop” and focus on things that are likely to be more impactful and stronger works. But this also comes from a somewhat convenient moral high ground, in the sense that it overly simplifies the effect that this would have on academia across different levels of experience and background. Yes, I have plenty of complaints about how conferences work now. I’ve already gotten my share of sloppy papers to review and even sloppier reviews to my own papers. I’m just worried about what would replace them, and who that replacement would work for.

On the surface, the idea of a crowdsourced filter sounds great. Instead of spending months only to get rejected by some AI agent, you could just put your work out there and let people judge it for themselves. The problem is that I don’t think this is how it would actually work in practice.

There is already an overwhelming amount of research being published every day on arXiv. People have thus turned to somewhat superficial indicators to decide what to spend their time on. Who wrote the paper? Where are they from? Do I recognize any of the names?

If someone like Yann LeCun puts his name on a paper, or even just posts something on Twitter, people will read it. But what if you’re an undergraduate at some random university? Nobody knows who you are and you don’t have a professor with thousands of followers to share your work. You can try to publish it on arXiv, maybe post a thread on Twitter, and hope that someone looks your way.

Maybe someone will. But I don’t think we should build a system around the assumption that they will.

I find it personally difficult to separate the value of publications from the opportunities that come with them. Sure, research shouldn’t be done for the sake of getting papers accepted. But telling someone who is just trying to get their foot in the door that they shouldn’t care about publications seems a little strange when the system that evaluates them hasn’t changed to match that.

It’s easy to say that publications don’t matter once you’ve reached a point where they don’t matter anymore.

And I don’t think it’s enough to tell people to “stop caring about publications” and to focus on doing “good work” when practically everyone else, from graduate admissions to hiring decisions, still rewards them. Until those incentives change too, we’re basically just making it harder for people without connections to compete.

I don’t think any of these problems are easy to solve. Academia is already struggling to keep up with the amount of research being produced, and I agree that something probably has to change. But I worry that when we talk about making academia “more efficient”, we’re mostly hearing from people who have already made it through the system. The people who haven’t even gotten their foot in the door don’t really have much of a say in what happens to it.

I guess this is where the title of this post comes in.

A lizard can detach its tail when threatened, sacrificing a part of itself to escape. And in some sense, it feels like that’s what’s happening with academia right now. The system is becoming difficult to sustain, and so we’re looking for parts that we can “afford” to get rid of.

For an established researcher, getting a paper accepted at a conference might just be like a formality, an opportunity to meet up and hang out with old friends on someone else’s money. They already know who to talk to and how to get people interested in their work. If they stopped submitting papers tomorrow and instead published everything on their personal website, I imagine they’d have no trouble getting people to read what they write.

But for someone trying to enter the field, getting accepted at conferences might be one of the only ways to get their work taken seriously. I, for one, didn’t get into research because someone saw that I was “good” and deserved an opportunity. I got in because I happened to know someone who knew someone. And I’m sure there are plenty of people who would have been just as capable as me, if not much more capable, who never got the same chance.

I think accessibility should be treated as something we actively try to preserve when reforming academia, rather than something we hope will improve as a consequence of fixing other problems.

The lizard might be able to survive without its tail. I’m not really convinced that everyone depending on the current academic system can afford to lose the same things.
entry.summary: Those in power stay in power

entry.title: Reflection: Pangram, Authenticity, and Me
entry.content:
I suppose it started back in middle school, which for me was back when Google Hangouts was a thing. I’m sure that sentence alone gave many people around my age shivers about their dark teenage days.

Middle school is a dark age for many, and with the power of the internet, there’s probably a lot more of our past out there than we’d like to admit. I envy those that lived in the age of lost media.

To start, I guess I should say that I was probably online a lot more than I should have been at my age. I wasn’t really aware of this until one day, when a friend mentioned to me:

Hey, you kind of talk like [Name of YouTuber].

Note that the name has been censored here to protect the right to privacy of my middle school self.

And this… concerned me. As much as I found this particular YouTuber entertaining to watch, it wasn’t someone I wanted to be identified with, frankly. Especially as a guy going through his teenage years at the peak of puberty.

This kept me up for days. What did that passing comment even mean? Was it my tone? My word choice? Was I using their catchphrases without even noticing? What was going on?

Before I knew it, I’d picked up some random person’s vibes just from watching so much of their content.

And I suppose, looking back, there have been many such cases throughout my life.

Until college, I pronounced “supermarket” with a shu because that’s how it was pronounced in Korean. I spoke (and still do, only worsened by the fact that I’ve been in London for the past month) with a slightly posh accent despite never having met a British person, much less having been anywhere near Europe or the UK. Needless to say, I was a big fan of Harry Potter growing up.

I guess the point I’m trying to get across is that we, as humans, are creatures of adaptation. We adapt to our surroundings, whether we’re aware of it or not. That’s our single biggest advantage in a world where countless predators are born much stronger and faster than us. We’ve survived by learning and adapting.

The words we use, the jokes we make, the way we react to things, even the opinions we hold. How much of that is really “ours”, and how much have we picked up from the people around us?

I guess one answer is that it’s the combination that matters. None of the individual pieces may be original, but the collection of them is.

And I think there’s something rather comforting about that.

Because otherwise, where do we draw the line? Am I no longer allowed to use a word because someone else used it “first”? Am I supposed to be embarrassed about having an accent? Am I supposed to go through my entire personality and try to figure out which parts are genuinely “mine” and which parts I “borrowed” from someone else?

Honestly, I doubt there would be much left by the end of it.

I think we’re a little too obsessed with the idea of being original. We want to be special, unique, a special little snowflake.

But what does any of that actually mean?

Take writing, for example. Everyone has their own writing style, or at least that’s what we like to think. But that style is something we’ve developed from years of reading other people’s work and being taught how to write in school. So how many people out there actually have their own writing style that is so unique that they have their own category?

Along that same line, I guess I don’t really understand the drama around Pangram and AI-generated content.

Yes, AI-generated content is often bad. We want good text. This is true.

People are out there saying things like “If my Pangram flags your Twitter post, I’m instantly blocking you”.

But good AI-generated text is good, even if it was written by an AI. We had “slop” before AI.

What is good is good, whatever the source. “Slop” is “slop”, whatever the source.

Would you ignore Shakespeare written by a monkey because it didn’t come from some old white guy?

On the other hand, you may be giving humanity a bit too much credit if you think the average person can write better than AI.

At the end of the day, who are you to throw the first stone?

People have become so hypercritical of AI-generated content that it’s almost become ridiculous. And it doesn’t stop there; anything remotely resembling AI-written content gets bashed as well.

AI-generated text from earlier generations contained a lot of em dashes. I know many people around me who were chased away from using em dashes because of these sorts of “witch hunts”.

Next came semicolons.

After that, it was very basic things we learned about how to write in English class, like the rule of three and other forms of clear technical writing.

Now people point at those same things and say that the text was generated by AI and is therefore not worth reading.

And again, the question is, what exactly are we asking people to do? At what point are we just asking people to be less like themselves so they can prove that they’re human?

Isn’t that a little backwards?

We’re so concerned with whether someone’s writing is “authentic” that we’re encouraging people to change the things that make their writing theirs.

If anything, this seems like the same insecurity I had back in middle school. I was so worried about sounding like someone else that it in turn made me less like myself. And now people are worried that sounding like AI makes them less human.

But why should we conform? Especially to standards set by… another AI? Not to throw shade on Pangram (I think the project in concept is really interesting and I’ve even tried training my own model for this to dive deeper!), it’s just that people are maybe using it in the wrong way for the wrong reasons.

I don’t think authenticity should require us to constantly prove that we haven’t been influenced by something else.

Not to say I’m supportive of all AI-generated content.

I, of course, think there are many places where AI has no place, regardless of quality. One example is institutions where the whole point is to have a human do the work, like in education.

I don’t think AI should be used to complete homework assignments. But I also think the reason it’s being used so much by students has a lot to do with the current education system rewarding only the top scores, with AI being an easier way to get there than actually being interested in the subject or assignment.

But that’s its own can of worms that I don’t want to get into here.

The point is that AI has its place.

And I think the question of authenticity becomes a little more complicated when we move from how we write to what we’re actually trying to express.

Modern performance art gets a lot of flak nowadays, with plenty of memes (which I admit I’ve enjoyed fully) being spawned from other people’s attempts at expressing what’s inside them.

But if we asked all of those people to paint a picture instead, it wouldn’t work the same way.

And for those who don’t have such talent in the currently accepted forms of art, these alternatives give them another venue to express themselves.

I think there’s room for different forms of expression, even ones that we personally don’t particularly like or understand ourselves.

And I suppose the same argument could be made for AI (hot take, I know).

Again, I’m not saying every piece of AI-generated content is meaningful, not any more than every painting or piece of writing is meaningful.

Of course, there’s a difference between someone using AI to express an idea they genuinely care about and someone generating a thousand posts just to fill the internet with content. I don’t think those are particularly comparable, even if both are technically AI-generated. Part of the gap is that current AI produces lower-quality content than humans by default, which may change as AI gets more powerful. And I think the bigger goal is to filter out low-quality content, human or not. In my humble opinion, it’s a somewhat naive take to conflate the two.

The question should be more about what they’re trying to express, rather than whose words or whose brushstrokes make up the components.

After all, we’ve always been borrowing from the world around us. The tools have changed, but I don’t think the fundamental question has.

All in all, I guess I’ve come a long way from being embarrassed about sounding like a YouTuber in middle school.

Though, to be fair, I still don’t think I’d particularly be thrilled if someone made the same comparison today.

And yet, here I am, years later, still speaking with the slightest tinge of an accent I have no claim over, using words I’ve learned from other people, and holding opinions that have probably been shaped by more random conversations, books, and experiences than I could ever hope to remember.

I mean, what can I say? We take things in just by living in the moment. Some of them may stick, others may not. We change, we grow, and occasionally we look back and wonder why on earth we used to talk like that.

We’re all products of the things we’ve consumed, whether we like it or not.

And now this will remain a part of you. You’re welcome.

entry.title: Reflection: My Experience at NeurIPS 2025 as an Undergrad Not Looking for a Job

link.title: Reflection: My Experience at NeurIPS 2025 as an Undergrad Not Looking for a Job

entry.content:
Before I went to NeurIPS, plenty of people warned me about what my first academic conference would be like. I didn’t think much of it at the time. This was academia, not a career fair. I assumed I wouldn’t be standing in line for an hour for a five-minute chat with someone who clearly didn’t want to be there, only to be told to scan a QR code and apply online.

I guess I had a naïve picture in my head of some 18th-century salon, where scholars in stuffy coats debated the truths of the world or whether the sun revolved around the moon. For the first day, that fantasy almost held up, minus the wigs. People were surprisingly bundled up for San Diego weather for some reason and the mood felt calm, almost contemplative.

Then I opened Twitter and realized I had missed the other half of the venue.

Source: Sergei Iakhnin on X

Everyone is on The Grind

For context, I went to NeurIPS as an undergrad about to graduate, with no plans to job hunt. My gap semester and summer were already booked with a research position in Tübingen, and after graduating in December I would technically be an independent researcher until grad school decisions came through. That made things socially awkward, but it also meant I wasn’t playing the same game as most of the people around me, and from the outside the game was easy to see.

There were a lot of people. I had been warned about the crowds, and I have been to packed events before, but nothing quite like this. The density was not just physical. It was social, professional, and relentlessly transactional. Quality conversation gave way to high-volume lead generation. Exchange LinkedIn. Scan the QR code. Grab the merch. Move on.

People asked questions to look interested, then slowly steered the conversation toward whether there were open positions. The ones who weren’t doing that sat along the walls with Overleaf and VS Code open, trying to get some work done during business hours. Nobody was discussing Kant. They were optimizing throughput.

On some level, I respect the hustle. But it wasn’t what I expected from an academic conference. The quant firms didn’t help, with their stock tickers flashing like miniature Wall Street installations. Everyone was busy executing, and almost nobody seemed to be stopping to think.

The Credential Filter

When everyone is searching for their next opportunity, heuristics become the dominant currency. School. Lab. Advisor. Company affiliation. You cannot bypass the filter.

The badge stare started right away. About 90 percent of the people I talked to, senior researchers and PhD students alike, spent most of the conversation looking at my badge instead of my face. When I said I was an undergrad, I could watch the interest drain out of them.

I know this will change as my career goes on. With a PhD and a stronger institution behind my name, the same words will probably land differently. But the whole thing left a bit of a sour taste. It felt objectifying, and it seemed almost designed to give everyone impostor syndrome. I’m not sure who benefits when nearly everyone walks away a little dissatisfied.

I had a first-author paper already published and more under review, and people treated me like a curiosity. “Nice, good job, you started early.” Then the conversation was over. There was no room to talk about the actual ideas. Twitter was full of posts about being open to “anything” and “meeting new people,” but a lot of attendees seemed to want something closer to prestige, or to be seen near a bigger name.

Academia, it turns out, is not immune to industry logic.

It did not help that I work in AI Safety. In practice, that often translates to “not reinforcement learning,” which was clearly the big gravitational center of the conference. Conversations followed a predictable decay: What school? Who is your advisor? What do you work on? At each step, more people disengaged. An undergrad, not from a famous lab, doing AI Safety instead of RL was simply not a high-value node.

Not to say everyone behaved this way. But enough did that the pattern became impossible to ignore.

The Real Signal Hides in the Niche

The trip wasn’t a total loss. The workshops were where I found what I came for.

The main conference often felt like an echo chamber, full of high-level talk about scaling and RL that everyone had already known for months. Workshops were different. They were small and focused, and the people there actually cared about the topic, because why else would they be in that room? Poster presenters and speakers were much more open to real discussion.

That’s where I finally found some of the scholarly energy I’d been looking for. The conversations went slower and deeper, and nobody was performing. I followed up with several people afterward, and a few of those could turn into real collaborations. None of that would have happened on the main stage.

NeurIPS wasn’t the philosophical retreat I’d imagined. It was closer to a battleground, where your name and your institution decide who pays attention to you. Still, it’s worth seeing the game clearly. I’d rather learn how it works now than find out years into the commitment.

At the very least, I now know what kind of fight I am choosing.
entry.summary: My eyes are up here, thanks.

entry.title: Creative: Blink and You’ll Miss It

link.title: Creative: Blink and You’ll Miss It

entry.content:
We live in an age of acceleration. Fast, fast, and faster. Trends flicker to life and vanish before we can even grasp them. Memes appear overnight, dominating conversations for mere days, then become relics before we’ve even fully appreciated whatever “skibidi” is supposed to be. In every conversation I’ve had at university, someone inevitably remarks, “This semester flew by, it feels like we just started.” It’s true; time has a strange way of slipping through our fingers.

A month and a half ago, I wrapped up my third year of college. Facing a full-time internship and juggling three research projects, I decided to spend the summer at home, freeing myself from the burden of cooking and housekeeping. Yet here I am, already realizing there’s just over a month left before I return for my final semester. It’s a scary thought: in a blink, it seems, this phase of my life, the one I spent most of my childhood preparing for, will be over.

Amidst all this chaos, it’s easy to lose sight of how beautiful life genuinely is, and not just in a cliché, motivational-poster kind of way. To keep myself grounded, I make sure to step away from my desk once a day, taking walks to breathe fresh air and observe the subtle changes around me. The new flowers blooming, birds darting through the sky, these reminders anchor me in the present.

When we’re inundated daily with endless streams of global news, it’s tempting to feel hopeless, caught in a narrative that the world is spiraling downward. But despite it all, the world remains profoundly good, rich with small moments worth savoring.

That’s why I created Blink. I needed a personal space to capture these transient thoughts, feelings, and observations in their raw form. In the past, I’d revisit journal entries from middle school and high school, deleting or editing moments I felt were “cringe” or insignificant. But looking back, I now realize those entries were honest reflections of my true self at the time, memories and emotions worth preserving, even if they feel awkward later.

The playlist songs I loved in middle school bring back warm, comforting memories today. Those seemingly trivial or embarrassing moments are essential parts of who I am. Blink is designed precisely to honor this truth: a minimalist, time-capsule journaling experience where entries lock permanently after 60 seconds—no edits, no deletions. It encourages authenticity, preserving the messy, beautiful, fleeting parts of life.

While I made this for myself and some friends, feel free to experience Blink for yourself, and celebrate the moments that make you uniquely you.

Try Blink Now

entry.title: Agentic AI: the new ‘groundbreaking technology’ of 2025

link.title: Agentic AI: the new ‘groundbreaking technology’ of 2025

entry.content:
Summary

Chain-of-thought and retrieval-augmented generation had their moments in 2022 and 2023. 2024 was reasoning models and multi-agent collaboration. 2025 is now agentic AI, and we may be onto something with this one. We’re five months into the chaos, so it’s a good time to look at what stuck and whether we should care.

What agentic AI is, and why people are excited

Agentic AI is the first real attempt to make AI more than a glorified autocomplete. A chatbot answers your prompt and stops. An agent gets a goal and keeps making decisions until it gets there, changing course when things go wrong. It works on its own and cooperates with other agents in a world that’s messy and unpredictable.

That’s a pretty big upgrade. For decades, AI was brought up to be the world’s most diligent intern: something that can work faster than humans without tiring. Agentic AI is the real step towards that, except it turned out to be more like an intern that starts their own company and then tries to automate your job. Think of a chess engine that suggests moves, versus one that signs itself up for a tournament and books its own flights.

The closest historical parallel I guess I can give is with the early Internet. Every network used to be its own little island, and nothing talked to anything else. Then TCP/IP and HTTP came along, and suddenly everything was connected. Agentic AI is at that same point right now. It’s fragmented and chaotic, and it might be about to turn into something huge.

Example: the travel-planning circus

Say you want to plan a five-day trip from Beijing to New York. The old way, a single agent works through flights, hotels and weather one at a time, like a very polite but slightly dim assistant. With agent protocols, you get the whole circus. Each of those jobs gets its own agent, and the agents negotiate until they agree on an itinerary.

The protocols differ in how they run the circus. MCP keeps things centralized and tidy. A2A and ANP let agents make deals across company lines. Agora, the most ambitious, lets agents agree on a structured protocol from plain-language descriptions, so they can work together without one being designed in advance.

The payoff is a system that can adapt on the fly when your plans (inevitably) change.

Not all interns are created equal

To understand agentic AI, you have to get used to the idea that “agent” covers a wide range. We’re nowhere close to perfecting this tech. At the shallow end you have simple reflex agents, like Roombas and rule-based chatbots. At the deep end you have multi-agent systems, where groups of specialized agents negotiate and bicker their way through complex tasks.

Most agentic systems today are a Frankenstein’s monster bolted together from the same parts. They take in data from whatever sources they can reach. They keep memory, both short-term context and long-term knowledge, sometimes with the recall of an elephant and sometimes with the recall of a goldfish. They break big, hairy tasks into small steps. They call tools like APIs and databases. They take real actions instead of just talking. And some of them learn over time, occasionally in ways their creators didn’t expect.

Like most of machine learning, a lot of this design copies God’s blueprints. Research on LLM memory borrows ideas like System 1 and System 2 thinking and theory of mind. Tool use exists because of human limits and specialization: we don’t do everything ourselves either. And I haven’t even mentioned the elephant in the room, which is that neural networks were inspired by brains in the first place.

Why agentic AI isn’t running the world (yet)

So why isn’t agentic AI running everything already? Because it’s hard. Really hard. Here are the main problems.

Standardization

Imagine everyone has their own agent, or their own team of agents. To be really useful, those agents need to talk to each other and work together. Right now they speak dialects so different that even Google Translate would give up. The lack of shared protocols is the bottleneck, and it’s the main thing keeping agentic AI from taking over the world (for now).

Security and privacy

The more freedom an agent has, the more you have to worry about what it does with your data. Authentication and access control are the bare minimum, not nice extras. Something something with great power comes great responsibility.

Reliability

An agent is only as good as its last meltdown. Remember the robot civil servant in Korea that drove itself down a flight of stairs after what looked like a rough day at work? In high-stakes settings, “works most of the time” isn’t good enough.

Evaluation

There’s no Consumer Reports for agentic AI (yet). Benchmarks are scattered, and everyone grades their own homework. Competitors end up calling each other out, and official reports get corrected and revised all the time.

Plugging in new tools

Plug-and-play is still a fantasy. Most integrations are brittle and manual, and setting them up is about as fun as assembling IKEA furniture with half the instructions missing. What you end up with is a mini helicopter running on three pig hooves on a train track. It might work for now, but it’s seconds away from falling apart.

Then there’s the human side, including the uneasy feeling that we might be building something we can’t fully control. We’ve all watched too many sci-fi movies, and that doesn’t help.

My take

What excites me most about agentic AI is the intentionality, much more than the buzzwords or the VC pitches. We’re finally building systems that chase goals and change plans mid-run, instead of just answering a prompt. That changes how we think about “intelligence” in machines. For the first time, it feels like we’re sketching something more than a tool. Something almost alive.

But I’m also wary.

People throw the word “agent” around a lot these days, usually without much rigor. Is a function-calling LLM with a planning loop and memory an agent? Technically, sure. So is a glorified macro if you squint hard enough. I think the harder problem is building agents that know where their competence ends. I want agents that can say “I don’t know” and hand the task to someone else. More capability is easy to sell. Knowing your limits is the frontier.

And honestly, a lot of what gets sold as agentic AI right now is old ideas with a new label: finite-state machines wrapped in Python with a “GPT” logo glued to the front. Cool demos, but that’s about it. People are closer to making movies than documentaries. If this field wants to survive the hype cycle, it needs fewer sizzle reels and more system audits, and more principled certification instead of vibes-based evaluation.

Still, I’m optimistic. Behind the noise are the researchers who are actually in the weeds, building new protocols and fixing stupid bugs at 2am. They’re the ones pulling the field forward, and most of them aren’t doing it for clout or paper count. They do it because they can see the outline of something real and strange.

and I want to be there when it shows up.

entry.title: Reflection: It Builds Character but
entry.content:
Maturity is often framed as a trifecta: biological, emotional, and psychological. Biologically, it’s about your body and brain catching up with the calendar. Emotional maturity? That’s when you can keep your cool even when someone cuts you off in traffic. Psychological maturity? It’s the ability to see beyond yourself—like realizing that maybe, just maybe, the world doesn’t revolve around your Spotify playlist.

The Early Days of “Maturity”

I can’t remember the first time someone told me I was mature for my age, but I do remember how it felt. Like winning an Oscar for Best Child Actor in the Drama of Life. While my classmates were busy arguing over whose Pokémon cards were cooler, I was sitting at the adult table, nodding along to conversations about mortgage rates and the price of gas. Not because I understood any of it—God no—but because it felt safer there. Kids my age were unpredictable, sometimes cruel. Adults, on the other hand? They liked me because I was quiet, polite, and didn’t cause trouble. I was their dream child—an old soul in a pint-sized body.

But here’s the thing about being an “old soul”: it’s lonely as hell. Sure, the adults liked me, but they were also adults. They weren’t going to invite me to play tag or trade snacks at recess. And the kids? They thought I was weird. Too serious. Too quiet. Too… something, I guess. So there I was, stuck in this no-man’s-land between childhood and whatever comes after. Really puts being a ‘young adult’ into perspective.

The Teenage Medal of Maturity

By my teenage years, being called mature for my age felt less like a compliment and more like a job description. I was supposed to be the one who had it all together.

Take high school, for example. While my friends were sneaking out to parties or stressing over prom dates, I was busy being the responsible one. The one who gave advice, who stayed sober so everyone else could get drunk without worrying about how they’d get home. And yeah, part of me took pride in that role—it felt good to be needed. But another part of me just wanted to scream: Can someone else be the adult for once?

The Ugly Truth About “Mature for Your Age”

For me, being “mature for my age” often meant coping with things I wasn’t ready for. It started when my family plopped me down in a country where I didn’t speak the language or understand the culture. To make things worse, they didn’t either. Suddenly, I wasn’t just a kid anymore. I was an interpreter, a mediator, a problem-solver. And I couldn’t exactly pick childhood back up where I’d left it.

Maybe you were forced into adulthood too soon. Maybe life gave you more funerals than birthday parties. Whatever the case, this so-called “maturity” often comes from enduring what no child—or adolescent—should have to. You get so used to being the bridge between worlds that you forget you were supposed to have solid ground of your own. Every conversation, every decision, every moment of uncertainty—you smooth it over, make it easier for everyone else. And in the process, you learn to shrink, to silence your own needs, because there’s never room for them when you’re too busy holding everything together.

Then one day, you look around and realize you don’t even know what it feels like to exist without carrying someone else’s weight. Being labeled “mature” doesn’t sound like a compliment anymore, does it?

The Turning Point

Now I’m 21 for some reason, and maturity is a reminder of everything I’ve been through to get here. It’s not something I wear with pride anymore; it’s something I carry with weariness. Because if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that maturity isn’t always earned—it’s often forced upon you by circumstances beyond your control.

And honestly? If I could go back and trade some of that maturity for a little more ignorance—a few more years of blind, uncomplicated joy—I would. Not because I don’t value what I’ve learned, but because some lessons come at too high a cost.

What Maturity Really Means

Maturity is often mistaken for composure, responsibility, or the ability to shoulder burdens without complaint. But at its core, it’s about perspective—about understanding yourself and the world in a way that makes sense of past and present.

But perspective is a double-edged sword. Sometimes it’s a gift, letting you see beyond yourself, helping you make sense of others. Other times, it’s a weight—one that distances you from the people around you, makes innocence feel like a language you can no longer speak. There are things you can only see because you don’t know any better—like believing in Santa Claus or thinking your high school crush is your soulmate.

When adults call a kid “mature,” I wonder what they’re praising. Maybe the kid is thoughtful. Maybe they’ve just learned not to ask for help. From the outside, the two can look pretty similar.

So if you ever meet someone who seems mature for their age, don’t just applaud them for it. Ask them how they’re really doing—because chances are, they’ve been carrying more than their fair share of weight for far too long. Give them room to be a kid. To explore without fear of judgment. To make mistakes without feeling like they’re letting everyone down.

And if you’re someone who’s been labeled “mature” your whole life? Take it from me: it’s okay to put down the armor every once in a while. To let yourself be messy and vulnerable and human. Because maturity isn’t about having all the answers—it’s about knowing when it’s okay not to have them at all.

So here’s to unlearning what we thought we knew about maturity, to giving ourselves permission to be—messy, reckless, human. And maybe to finding some joy in the process.
entry.summary: Because you can look back but you can't go back

entry.title: Opinion: Escapism, complacency, and the inner Gigachad

link.title: Opinion: Escapism, complacency, and the inner Gigachad

entry.content:
From zero to hero: why we root for losers now

Once upon a time, our heroes were untouchable. They wore tuxedos to gunfights, jumped off skyscrapers without breaking a sweat, and had powers that made the gods of old look almost underwhelming. We looked up to them and wanted to be them. Lately, something strange has been happening. Our protagonists aren’t flawless anymore. They’re… well, kind of losers? A struggling mom saves the multiverse. A high schooler turns into an edgy anti-hero. A socially awkward anime girl can only talk by writing in a flipbook. What happened? Did we all decide that being cool is overrated?

My guess is it’s some mix of disillusionment and a desperate need to escape. When the economy is stuck and social pressure is heavy, we seem to have swapped aspirational fantasies for something more relatable: flawed characters who stumble their way to greatness. Is that empowering, or are we just fooling ourselves with prettier versions of mediocrity?

Why we love watching nobodies become somebodies

Take isekai. It’s a genre common in modern Japanese pop culture where a character gets pulled into another world (think The Matrix, but with more swords and arguably worse-written existential crises). The whole genre runs on one premise: losers get a second chance. The socially inept gamer becomes an overpowered hero. The book-obsessed psychopath razzle-dazzles medieval peasants with modern knowledge. The fantasy is simple. You escape your current life and start over as someone extraordinary.

Western media loves this trope too. Remember Ready Player One? A broke, awkward kid saves the virtual universe because he knows obscure 80s trivia. Or Harry Potter: an unloved boy living under the stairs finds out he’s a wizard destined to beat the most feared dark lord in history. These stories land because most of us secretly hope we’re meant for something bigger than our boring lives. We’re only so many days away from our own breakthrough.

The catch is that these stories often cheat. The protagonist doesn’t win because they work hard or grow as a person. They win because they’re “chosen,” or because they trip over godlike powers. That’s escapism at its most fun, and also at its most dangerous.

When escapism becomes a trap

These stories look empowering at first. Even the most flawed of us can be great! Look closer, though, and a lot of them romanticize passivity.

Back to isekai. The protagonist usually gets huge power without earning it. One minute they’re a nobody; the next, they’re fighting zombies or saving the world from some guy with a hand fetish. Fun to watch, sure. But what’s the message? That greatness takes no effort? That you just wait for a deus ex machina to fix your life?

This shows up outside fantasy too. A lot of modern media sells “acceptance” in a way that slides into complacency. Characters get celebrated for “being themselves,” and nobody asks them to grow. The worst offender is the “romance with a gimmick” show. These shows decided that drama and a slow build to a real relationship took too long. So we get the same formula every season: Girl A has a quirk, she meets Boy A, and they live happily ever after. It’s like we collectively decided that wanting something in life and working towards it was too much work.

And maybe that’s the point. When real problems feel impossible to fix, we reach for stories that let us off the hook. Escapism helps for a while. But it can also widen the gap between what we expect from life and what we actually get.

The case for struggle: why we might need to suffer

Growth hurts. That’s kind of the point. Magical thinking and escapist fantasies can’t replace hard work and sticking with it, and deep down we know this. That’s why Rocky and Good Will Hunting still hit. Nobody in those movies gets handed anything. They fight for it.

So how do we square this with our love of loser-to-hero stories? By rethinking what “acceptance” means. Accepting yourself should mean being honest about where you are right now and still trying to get better. Giving up on getting better is resignation, and we shouldn’t call it acceptance.

What if media leaned into that? Picture an isekai where the hero gets no instant godlike powers and has to learn the new world from scratch. Picture flawed characters who inspire us by working for their success, so we see what we could become if we actually tried. That’s how you go even further beyond.

Unleashing your inner Gigachad

Enter Korea’s first viral meme of 2025: the Inner Gigachad. It started as a joke about acting absurdly confident while the world burned around us, and it quickly turned into a rallying cry for self-improvement. People filled their feeds with posts in a mix of broken English and Korean, held together by pure charisma, next to pictures of chiseled men and captions like “Hey 만삣삐, you have to trust yourself to take action. Only you can decide what the right decision is.”

It was ridiculous and completely over the top, and it worked. The Inner Gigachad never asked you to be perfect. It asked you to believe in yourself with total audacity, even when you felt like a loser. You show up to life with the swagger of someone who thinks they’re invincible, even if you’re barely holding it together.

So maybe you won’t save the multiverse or lead a rebellion against a dystopian regime. Maybe your story is smaller and quieter, and it still counts. Learning a new skill, mending a broken relationship, getting out of bed on a day when everything feels impossible: those are real fights. So STOP 띵킹 만삣삐. A day will come when your hard work pays off, and it won’t be some benevolent god who rewards you. It’ll be you.
entry.summary: Because sometimes you need the stick more than the carrot

entry.title: Opinion: The problem with ‘positivity culture’
entry.content:
The future is (not) bright: toxic positivity in a doomer world

It’s 2024, and the future looks grim. The world is on fire (literally), people are stealing doors from public bathrooms for some internet points, and your dream job in tech has taken your self-esteem and any hope of a career hostage. The game seems to be rigged from the start but the stakes are high. But hey, stay positive! If you aren’t projecting perfect, sunshine-filled happiness, are you even trying?

So here we are, stuck in a bit of a paradox. On one side, a generation of “doomers” is hell-bent on telling everyone how hopeless things are (thanks, Zoomers). On the other, toxic positivity keeps trying to “fix” the world with a hashtag and a wellness retreat.

…Right.

Doomer culture: the kids are all right, except they’re not

Spend five minutes on Twitter (now called X for some reason?) and you’ll see Gen Z and Gen Alpha doing what they do best: predicting the end of the world. I mean, what can I say? They’ve inherited a planet that’s boiling, a job market that treats them like a joke, and an economy where “getting by” feels out of reach. The generation before them gaslit them for years, and now they shake their heads and wait for it all to implode.

So of course they live in a permanent existential crisis. How could they not? The world keeps promising solutions that turn out to be slicked-up scams, and the people making decisions are old men who look like they’d send Morse code by clattering their loose dentures.

Take tech for one. The opportunities are endless! So are the fake job postings. Companies found the “FREE MONEY HACK” people have been talking about for ages: post listings for jobs that don’t exist and collect tax credits. A dystopian version of corporate charity. If you somehow land an interview, expect to be ghosted for weeks, then get a call at 3 pm from a blocked number on a Friday asking whether you have 5+ years of experience for an entry-level role. If they haven’t hung up on you by the third question, you’ll be the one who wants off the call. To make things worse, half the time the interviewers don’t even know what job they’re hiring for. They read off a script and pretend “What’s your greatest weakness?” is a real question to ask a grown adult.

I get it, doomers. It’s hard to stay optimistic in a system that seems built to make you fail. But this negativity, valid as it feels, builds a toxic echo chamber. If everyone is stuck in the “we’re doomed” spiral, how does anyone get out? The system may suck, but not trying to change it helps nobody.

Toxic positivity: “good vibes only” for the already privileged

At the other end sits “toxic positivity”. I mean, even the name feels contradictory: what do you even get when you combine something negative with something positive? Unfortunately the operator is multiplication. It’s everywhere too, waiting to tell you that a bit more “positive thinking” and some “good vibes hehe XD” will solve your problems.

Positivity itself is fine. I love positivity. I’d have it for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. The problem is believing that if we all slap on a smile and repeat “everything will be okay,” the world will rearrange itself into something pristine. Pretending things are fine when they aren’t just makes them worse.

You’re struggling. I’m struggling. Little Timmy down the street is four and he’s struggling. Yet you’re supposed to act like you’re on a permanent vacation, crystal-clear water and sunset included. You can’t let anyone see that you’re stressed and lost, because people won’t care, or worse, they’ll use it against you. Every interaction gets scrutinized, and any sign of vulnerability counts as an admission of failure. So you bottle it up and keep the facade intact. You post filtered selfies that probably wouldn’t pass Face ID, and you pray your self-doubt doesn’t catch up.

When you have to act “fine” all the time, there’s no room to be real. Nobody gets to say “I’m struggling, and that’s okay.” You get an endless loop of “good vibes only :))” mantras that just feed the feeling that you’re not enough.

The echo chamber of negativity

This is where the doomers and the good-vibes crowd end up in the same place. Turns out two negatives don’t make a positive here. Each group sits in its own echo chamber and feeds its own worst instincts. Doomers trade memes about drowning in student debt and climate change. The positivity crowd trades hashtags about manifesting success.

Where does that end? The doomers’ fear grows when everyone around them shares it. The good-vibes crowd’s refusal to look at reality leaves everyone else feeling like they’re missing something, like maybe they’re the ones doing it wrong.

Both sides miss the point. The answer isn’t one or the other. It’s a messy, ugly “both.”

You’re struggling, I’m struggling, and that’s okay

Life isn’t going to be perfect. Positive thinking won’t change the fact that the system is broken, the job market is broken, and your social media posts aren’t fixing either. Everyone has bad stretches, and a lot of us feel like society was designed to make us fail.

So don’t pretend it’s sunshine and rainbows when it clearly isn’t. Let yourself feel the bad stuff. The belief that good vibes fix everything is toxic because it keeps us away from the root problems. You can’t heal if you won’t look at what’s wrong, and you can’t fix a system while you’re busy pretending it works.

Maybe we should take a page from Inside Out: the one where Sadness, Anger, and Fear turn out to matter as much as Joy. Each of them has a job in how we deal with the world.

Final thoughts: authenticity over positivity

So what’s the fix? Stop pretending. If you’re struggling, say so. Your emotions are part of being human, so stop trying to patch them like bugs. Honesty is the best tool we have for getting through this godforsaken world. It won’t change the world overnight, but it might leave us better equipped to survive it.

And no, that doesn’t mean everything will be okay. Even with this “solution,” there’s no guarantee of a happy ending. That’s life.
entry.summary: Because toxic positivity may actually be harming us

entry.title: Reflection: The Country Mouse Goes to New York

link.title: Reflection: The Country Mouse Goes to New York

entry.content:
The country mouse goes to New York

You probably know the fable. The country mouse goes to the city, expects the good life, and finds it loud, overwhelming, and full of surprises. After a few years among the Illinois cornfields, I thought I understood that mouse pretty well. I did not expect to become him on a trip to New York for the LIFEPLUS conference. The city had plans for me: cold weather, expensive food, and enough mishaps for a short stand-up set.

The cornfield mindset

Champaign is, let’s say, “charmingly slow-paced.” Life here is Walmart runs, the occasional Target splurge, and more corn than anyone needs. I’ve spent a lot of time wishing for more: more to do, more energy, more… life. So when I got invited to LIFEPLUS in New York City, I thought this was it. My big moment.

I pictured myself slipping right into the hustle, soaking up the glamor like I’d lived there for years. What I got was a string of reminders that I am a country mouse through and through.

My wallet vs. the city

First, the pizza. I wanted the classic New York slice: greasy, floppy, eaten standing on a sidewalk. I’d seen enough Spider-Man movies to know pizza was a requirement for being a real New Yorker, right up there with complaining about the weather and pretending to enjoy a packed bar. Was the real thing as glamorous as the movies? I honestly can’t tell you.

I squeezed through the crowd and ended up at Joe G Pizza (not to be confused with Joe’s Pizza), staring at a $30 menu and the mustache of a nice old Italian man, also named Joe. The pizza was 80% crust and 20% financial regret. If you’ve ever stood in an aisle debating two loaves of bread over a six-cent difference, you know the kind of heartbreak I mean.

Then there were the buses. I got off at the wrong stop twice. The first time, I waited over an hour in the freezing cold before I realized I was at the stop for buses going the other way. The second time was the same story, with extra frostbite. The only thing keeping the city from swallowing me whole was an EDM Buddhist mantra I found myself singing(?) along to as it got dark and my patience ran out. Om mani padme hum indeed.

The LIFEPLUS conference

Even with all the hiccups, the conference was everything I’d hoped for. Hanwha knows how to throw a party: live performances, endless trays of finger food, and an open bar that made me feel like I’d wandered into the VIP section of life. I took a bite of some caviar hors d’oeuvre (French for “the good stuff”) and for a second I swear my net worth went up. It was the kind of taste that makes you rethink every budget meal you’ve ever eaten.

But the best part (really!) was seeing people from my internship again. It reminded me that the world is mostly good, and that maybe I should trust it a bit more. I met new people too, from all kinds of backgrounds, and the conversations felt easy and warm. I’ve been to enough meetups where everyone stays in their own little huddle to know how rare that is. Here, talking to strangers just felt natural.

Did I overdo it? Absolutely. Four cocktails, two glasses of wine, and half a bottle of beer later, my face was starting to swell (thanks, alcohol intolerance). To be fair, the half-bottle of beer had already maxed out my alcohol meter. Everything after that went toward my social battery. Even through the haze of bad decisions, I couldn’t stop smiling. It was a really good night, especially with two midterms and a final project behind me.

The squirrels of Champaign

Still, as much as I loved the conference, I felt more at home walking the quiet streets of Champaign. I like watching two squirrels chase each other up a tree. I like the crunch of gravel under my shoes.

New York is bright and exciting, and it wore me out. I get excited about the weekly Aldi Finds. I hesitate before splurging on eggs. I’m happiest under open sky with empty fields around me. For someone like that, home is where life moves a little slower.

I left my comfort zone, and I came back liking what I have a lot more. The country mouse in me is staying put.
entry.summary: Because I prefer my plain food and simple life in the country

entry.title: Reflection: Art and the Search for Greener Grass

link.title: Reflection: Art and the Search for Greener Grass

entry.content:
The Dream That Wasn’t

In the quiet corners of my childhood, art was my secret portal to worlds unseen. Crayons in hand, I’d sketch adventures where I battled mythical beasts and, naturally, emerged the hero. I loved being able to invent a world and invite other people into it. For a while, I thought I might do that for a living.

Yet, as the years passed, whispers of doubt began to cloud the vibrant landscape. It didn’t take long before the vivid scenes I created were overshadowed by the looming shadows of reality. The dream of becoming an artist and inviting others to my world quietly retreated into the background, replaced by the more “sensible” paths that adulthood seemed to demand. And without the courage or confidence to stand my ground, I could only watch as the treehouse of dreams was replaced with iron bars that drew a line across the horizon. The artist inside me was boxed up, sealed away, while the world told me it was time to “grow up” and “get real.”

Get in the F*cking Robot

When you grow up doubting every decision, the world has a way of making choices for you. Computer science came pre-packaged with stability and parental approval. I went along with it, and each calculated step forward made the next one seem inevitable. It felt safe. But in the background, there was always the nagging feeling that I wasn’t being brave enough to make my own choices. I wasn’t living; I was just existing in a box that someone else had drawn.

I couldn’t trust myself to take big bets. While others chased dreams, I measured cliffs, calculated the drop, and convinced myself that staying put was wisdom rather than cowardice. I’d become very good at rationalizing my own fears.

The Other Side

My internship at Hanwha made that harder to ignore. I met students from all sorts of backgrounds, including people pursuing the arts. They had the training and talent to go after what they wanted, but what I envied was their confidence. They spoke about those futures as real possibilities, even without a guarantee that things would work out. I wondered what it would have been like to grow up thinking that way.

One friend had moved abroad to attend an art high school in America. It sounded like the premise of a Hallmark movie. My family moved frequently when I was growing up, and I remembered moving rather differently. Each time, I left behind friends and whatever little life I’d managed to build. For my friend, moving was a choice made for something they loved. For me, it was something that happened without warning. You could call that a difference in perspective, but there’s a world of difference between choosing to move and being told you’re moving.

Naturally, I started thinking about the “what ifs.” What if I’d asked my family to move for my own artistic ambitions? Then I remembered a recent conversation in which I joked that, if I ever won the lottery, I’d major in the arts. My family laughed. Maybe they didn’t mean much by it, but I couldn’t help wondering what would have happened if I’d said it seriously. Even in a hypothetical world where money wasn’t an issue, art was still the punchline.

The Grass We Water

But here’s the thing about looking over the fence: you miss the garden dying at your feet. I remember a time when I was so caught up in “what-ifs” that I nearly forgot to water my own plants. Literally. My poor houseplants were wilting while I daydreamed about alternate timelines where I’m someone I’m not and do things that, deep down, I know I would never do even if the opportunity came up. But reality has a way of snapping you back—like when you realize your once-thriving fern is now a crispy relic of negligence.

It was then that I realized, maybe that’s okay. The imperfection part, not the houseplants. Maybe the point isn’t to bemoan the paths not taken, but to understand why we chose the ones we did. Sometimes, it’s easier to fantasize about being a different person than it is to embrace who you are and the decisions that led you here. Maybe the real challenge isn’t in wishing we were someone else—it’s in accepting who we are now and finding ways to bloom where we’re planted.

That doesn’t mean I was wrong to mourn the paths I never got to explore. Some choices weren’t entirely mine in the first place. But I don’t want to spend the rest of my life arguing with the person I might have been. I’ve still got the person I am, and that person could use a little attention.

I used to think the grass was always greener on the other side. Maybe it’s greener where you water it. My fern would certainly have appreciated that insight earlier.

I may have traded my crayons for a bunch of zeros and ones, but I haven’t entirely lost what I liked about art: making something that didn’t exist before. Computer science gives me some room for that, and art doesn’t have to be my career to have a place in my life.

So maybe the grass I once dreamed of is no longer the one I water. But that doesn’t mean I can’t make this garden beautiful, in my own way, with the tools I have.
